title: How long does $500,000 last?
hook: You take $40,000 a year from savings that keep earning. When does the money run out?

knows: interest is charged first in the minimum-payment trap (minimum-payment-trap)
doesNotKnow: that a pot that keeps earning while you draw from it lasts longer than pot ÷ withdrawal, and forever if you take no more than its interest

objective: The learner can explain that $500,000 earning 5% while $40,000 a year is withdrawn lasts 20.1 years, not 12.5, because the interest ($25,000 in year 1) pays part of every withdrawal; taking only the interest leaves the pot unchanged.

claims.text: $500,000 earning 5% a year, with $40,000 taken out at the end of each year, lasts 20.1 years (20 full withdrawals and part of a 21st).
claims.source: n = −ln(1 − rP/W) / ln(1 + r) = −ln(1 − 0.05 × 500,000 / 40,000) / ln 1.05 = −ln 0.375 / 0.04879 = 20.10. Stepping b ← b × 1.05 − 40,000: year 20 balance 4,013, year 21 would be negative. Demo.tsx life(), path(); builder node run 2026-10-14. Brief: company/domains/briefs/economics.md #63.
claims.note: Derivation: n = -ln(1 - 0.05 x 500/40)/ln 1.05 = 20.103; stepping gives 20 full withdrawals with $4,011 left (the source note says $4,013: a typo, not learner-facing), then a partial 21st. artifacts/fact-check-wave-j/wj-econ-phys-math-geo/sav.mjs.

claims.text: In year 1 the pot earns $25,000, so after the $40,000 withdrawal it shrinks by only $15,000.
Each year the pot earns a little less, so the end speeds up.
claims.source: Interest is 5% of a falling balance, so the yearly fall W − 0.05 × b grows as b shrinks; the stage line steepens toward zero (Demo.tsx path()).
claims.note: Derivation: the yearly fall is W - 0.05b, which grows as b shrinks, so the drawn line steepens toward zero.

claims.text: Taking $25,000 a year, exactly the interest, the pot stays at $500,000 and never runs out.
claims.note: Derivation: 500,000 x 1.05 - 25,000 = 500,000 every year; life(25, 5) = Infinity, readout 'never runs out'.

claims.text: At 0% growth, $40,000 a year lasts 12.5 years: division is only right when the money earns nothing.
claims.source: 500,000 / 40,000 = 12.5; for any r > 0, −ln(1 − rP/W)/ln(1 + r) > P/W. Demo.tsx life(40, 0). Other slider values at 5%: $30k 36.7, $50k 14.2, $60k 11.1 years.
claims.note: Arithmetic and derivation: 500/40 = 12.5. For r > 0, -ln(1 - x) > x and ln(1 + r) < r, so n > (rP/W)/r = P/W: division undercounts whenever the money earns. Slider values at 5%: $30k 36.7, $50k 14.2, $60k 11.0 years.

claims.text: A steady 5% is a made-up rate; real returns vary. The model has end-of-year withdrawals and no inflation, taxes or fees; not a plan or advice.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx path(); reveal's last sentence; stage chip 'Grows 5% a year, then you withdraw.' Brief keeps any 'safe withdrawal rate' rule out of learner text.
claims.note: Lesson rule: path() has a constant rate, end-of-year withdrawals and no inflation, tax or fee terms. Stage note (not a claim): at $20k a year the balance passes the chart's $600k top in year 15 and is then drawn flat along the top edge (py clamps at BMAX); the readout correctly says 'never runs out'.

recall.question: A pot of $200,000 earns 4% a year. You take out $8,000 at the end of every year. How long does it last?
options: Forever: $8,000 is exactly the yearly interest
recall.why: 4% of $200,000 is $8,000, so each year's interest pays the whole withdrawal and the pot never shrinks. Division ignores what the money earns.
